value: The guide lists six such limits in all, including limits on how long an algorithm is used and on the time available for attacks; these are the first two.
reason: SP 800-57 Pt 1 §5.3 (p. 47) numbers six limits, not four.

value: What does the container security guide (Special Publication 800-190) say the ephemeral, automated nature of container management may not fit?
reason: The guide never defines 'ephemeral computing'; it only says the ephemeral and automated nature of container management may not fit traditional asset management (§4.5, p. 46). The front now asks only what the source says.

value: The asset-management policies and tools an organisation has traditionally used.
reason: Back follows the reworded front; the old back offered a circular definition the source does not give.

value: The guide raises this under incident response, because responders must still know each container's role, owner and sensitivity however briefly it runs.
reason: Says why it matters, using the same passage (§4.5, p. 46).

value: As one example of a provider platform, beside IaaS, PaaS, SaaS and container as a service, where responsibility likely follows a shared model.
reason: SSDF p. 12 says it 'likely follows a shared responsibility model'; the old back dropped 'likely'.

value: The framework does not define serverless. It names it as a delivery model where responsibility for secure development practices may be split, so the tenant should agree with providers who does each task.
reason: The old explanation said the framework 'expects' shared responsibility; the source says responsibility 'may be distributed' and the tenant should set up an agreement naming the responsible party for each practice and task (p. 12).

value: Like hiring a staffed kitchen for an event: you bring the recipes, the venue runs the ovens, and an agreement says who cleans what.
reason: 'By the dish' implied pay-per-use billing, which the cited source does not say.

value: In the container security guide, where should a container's persistent data be kept, rather than written to its root file system?
reason: The guide never calls root-file-system writes 'ephemeral storage'; it says persistence should come from external stores (§2.2, p. 16). The front no longer asserts that premise.

value: In external, persistent data stores, because containers are meant to be immutable.
reason: Back follows the reworded front.

value: The guide names databases and cluster-aware persistent volumes. Anything written only inside the container is therefore temporary, which this deck calls ephemeral storage.
reason: Separates the source's words from the deck's own term.

value: Pre-image resistance: no one can feasibly find a message that produces a given hash value, such as the published digest.
reason: The attacker must match a digest that is already fixed, which is the guide's pre-image resistance (SP 800-57 Pt 1 §4.1, p. 40); leading with collision resistance gave two answers.

value: The digest is fixed in advance, so a forger needs a new image that produces it, which pre-image resistance makes infeasible; collision resistance covers finding any two matching messages.
reason: Explains why the fixed digest makes pre-image resistance the answer.

value: A breakdown of the safeguards meant to keep tenants apart, for example in stored data, memory, network routing or even reputation.
reason: Tier C (ENISA): the old back followed the source sentence almost word for word; now in our own words.

value: The agency links the risk to multi-tenancy and shared resources, which it calls defining features of cloud computing, but notes such attacks are rarer and harder than attacks on ordinary operating systems.
reason: Adds the agency's own caveat from the same passage (p. 9), in our own words.

value: Containers should be deployed but not changed, and are replaced when updated; virtual machines are usually reconfigured and upgraded throughout their life.
reason: SP 800-190 p. 16: containers 'should be operated as stateless entities that are deployed but not changed'; the back stated it as a fact.

value: In an IaaS cloud, by contrast, consumers can run one or more guest operating systems virtualised on a single physical host.
reason: 'Only' is not in SP 500-292 p. 16, which says 'An IaaS cloud allows one or multiple guest OS's to run virtualized on a single physical host.'

value: The standard's terms section (clause 3.1.5) also borrows a wider definition from another international recommendation: two or more systems exchanging information and mutually using what was exchanged.
reason: The general definition is borrowed from ITU-T Y.101 in clause 3.1.5 (p. 7). It is not the standard's own definition.

value: Which provider sub-role makes sure the customer's and provider's information security policies are aligned and meet the SLA's security requirements?
reason: Y.3502 clause 8.3.1.7 (p. 21): policies must 'meet the security requirements stated in the SLA', not the SLA as a whole.

value: FIPS 140-3 also changes some of that standard's annexes, which the Cryptographic Module Validation Program may do as a validation authority.
reason: The old sentence ('as the validation programme is allowed to as a validation authority') has to be read twice.

value: The catalogue says common secure configurations are also known as hardening guides, and the settings chosen become part of the system's configuration baseline.
reason: CM-6 never defines hardening. It links the term only through 'hardening guides' (p. 130), and the card should show that link.

value: The adversary learns about one record's presence in the training data, not how the model itself works.
reason: 'Only' overstated: SP AI 100-2 p. 42 adds that membership inference can be a building block for data extraction.

value: ITU-T Y.3500 | ISO/IEC 17788:2014, Cloud computing: Overview and vocabulary, clauses 3.2.27 and 3.2.37, PDF pp. 9 and 10
reason: Clause 3.2.37 (tenant) is on PDF p. 10, not p. 9.

value: ITU-T Y.3500 | ISO/IEC 17788:2014, Cloud computing: Overview and vocabulary, clauses 3.2.35 and 3.2.13, PDF pp. 10 and 8
reason: Clause 3.2.13 (derived data, including logs) is on PDF p. 8, not p. 10.
